title: High-quality CPR, AED use, and choking relief
objective: Perform high-quality CPR on adults, children and infants, operate an AED safely, and apply the correct choking relief technique for each age group.
body:
Once you recognize cardiac arrest, the quality of your CPR strongly affects survival. HOSA scenarios test the specific numbers and how they change with the patient's age.

**High-quality adult CPR.** Place the heel of one hand on the center of the chest (lower half of the breastbone) with the other hand on top. Push at a **compression rate** of 100 to 120 per minute and a **compression depth** of at least 2 inches (5 cm) but not more than 2.4 inches. Allow full **chest recoil** after each push so the heart can refill, and minimize interruptions, keeping pauses under 10 seconds. Use a ratio of 30 compressions to 2 breaths. Open the airway with the **head-tilt, chin-lift** and give each breath over about 1 second, just enough to make the chest rise. Rescuers should switch compressors about every 2 minutes because fatigue reduces quality.

**Children and infants.** For a child (age 1 to puberty), compress about 2 inches using one or two hands. For an infant (under 1 year), compress about 1.5 inches (4 cm) in the center of the chest just below the nipple line. A single rescuer of an infant uses the two-thumb encircling-hands technique or the heel of one hand and a 30:2 ratio; with two rescuers, use 15:2 for children and infants. If you are alone and did not see a child collapse, give about 2 minutes of CPR before leaving to call 911 if you have no phone.

**Using an AED.** Turn it on as soon as it arrives and follow the voice prompts.
1. Expose and dry the chest.
2. Attach pads in the pictured positions.
3. Make sure no one touches the person while the AED analyzes.
4. Say "clear" and press shock if advised.
5. Resume compressions immediately after the shock.

Use pediatric pads for children under 8 when available; if not, adult pads are acceptable as long as they do not touch. Avoid placing pads directly over an implanted device.

**Choking.** A person who can cough forcefully should be encouraged to keep coughing. Signs of severe obstruction include inability to speak or breathe, a weak cough and clutching the throat. For a responsive adult or child, current guidelines call for cycles of 5 back blows followed by 5 **abdominal thrusts** (Heimlich maneuver) just above the navel; use chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts for pregnant or very large people. For an infant, alternate 5 back blows and 5 chest thrusts; never use abdominal thrusts on an infant. If the person becomes unresponsive, start CPR and look in the mouth for an object before giving breaths, removing it only if you see it.

The most common mistake students make is mixing up age-specific numbers, such as using adult compression depth or abdominal thrusts on an infant.
examples: Two classmates perform CPR on a coach; they switch compressors at the 2-minute AED analysis to keep compressions deep and fast.
A 7-month-old cannot cry or cough after eating; the rescuer gives 5 back blows followed by 5 chest thrusts.
After the AED delivers a shock, the rescuer immediately resumes compressions instead of checking for a pulse.

questions.stem: During adult CPR, a rescuer leans on the chest between compressions. Why is this a problem?
choices: It makes compressions too fast
It prevents full chest recoil so the heart cannot refill
It causes the AED to malfunction
It increases the compression depth too much
questions.explanation: Leaning prevents recoil, reducing blood refilling the heart. It does not directly change rate, which is the main distractor.

questions.stem: What compression rate is recommended for adult CPR?
choices: 60 to 80 per minute
80 to 100 per minute
120 to 140 per minute
100 to 120 per minute
questions.explanation: Current guidelines call for 100 to 120 compressions per minute; 120 to 140 is too fast to allow good depth and recoil.

questions.stem: A lone rescuer is giving CPR to an infant. What compression-to-breath ratio should be used?
questions.explanation: A single rescuer uses 30:2 for all ages. The 15:2 ratio is used only when two rescuers treat a child or infant.

questions.stem: The AED has just delivered a shock. What should the rescuer do next?
choices: Check for a pulse for 10 seconds
Remove the pads
Immediately resume chest compressions
Wait for the AED to reanalyze
questions.explanation: Compressions resume right after a shock; the AED will reanalyze in about 2 minutes. Pausing for a pulse check adds harmful interruption.

questions.stem: A man in a restaurant clutches his throat and cannot speak or cough. What is the best action?
choices: Give cycles of 5 back blows and 5 abdominal thrusts until the object comes out or he becomes unresponsive
Encourage him to keep coughing
Give him water to drink
Perform a blind finger sweep
questions.explanation: Inability to speak or cough means severe obstruction, treated with repeated cycles of back blows and abdominal thrusts. Encouraging coughing is only appropriate when he can cough forcefully.

questions.stem: A 4-month-old is choking and cannot breathe. Which technique is correct?
choices: Abdominal thrusts
5 back blows alternated with 5 chest thrusts
Blind finger sweeps
Chest thrusts only with two hands
questions.explanation: Infants receive back blows and chest thrusts. Abdominal thrusts risk injuring an infant's organs and are not used.

questions.stem: You need to use an AED on a 5-year-old but only adult pads are available. What should you do?
choices: Do not use the AED
Cut the adult pads to fit
Use the adult pads, making sure they do not touch
Place both pads on the back
questions.explanation: Adult pads are acceptable when pediatric pads are unavailable, as long as they do not touch. Withholding the AED removes the child's best chance.

questions.stem: A choking woman who is visibly pregnant becomes unable to breathe. What is the best modification?
choices: Use chest thrusts instead of abdominal thrusts
Use back blows only
Give abdominal thrusts lower on the abdomen
Lay her down and wait for EMS
questions.explanation: Chest thrusts avoid pressure on the pregnant abdomen. Abdominal thrusts, even placed lower, could harm the mother and fetus.

flashcards.definition: The speed of chest compressions: 100 to 120 per minute for all ages.
At least 2 inches (5 cm) for adults, about 2 inches for children and about 1.5 inches (4 cm) for infants.
Letting the chest return fully to its normal position between compressions so the heart can refill.
A maneuver that opens the airway by tilting the head back and lifting the chin.
Inward and upward thrusts just above the navel used to relieve severe choking in adults and children.
